summary: This standards-track memo defines an IP option that tells routers along a packet's path to look at it more closely than usual. It is useful for protocols that need routers to process certain packets even though they are not addressed to the router.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 2113 defines an IP option, a small field in the packet header, that asks routers along the path to examine a packet more closely even though it is not addressed to them. Protocols that need special router processing, such as RSVP and IGMP, use it. Routers that do not understand the option simply forward the packet as usual.

subtitle: An IP option that tells routers to look more closely at a packet that is not addressed to them.

tldr.problem: Protocols such as RSVP need routers along the path to intercept packets not addressed to them, but changing the main forwarding path could cost too much performance.
tldr.mechanism: The Router Alert IP option (option number 20, length 4) marks a packet so routers that recognize it examine it more closely, while ordinary forwarding stays untouched.
tldr.outcome: It lets protocols such as RSVP and IGMP get router attention cheaply during gradual deployment. It has been updated by RFC 5350 and RFC 6398.

today: RFC 2113 is a Proposed Standard. It was updated by RFC 5350 and RFC 6398 and has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: Why Routers Need an Alert
sections.content:
New routing protocols often couple loosely to existing unicast routing, which lets them deploy without reinventing basic routing functions, but it means they can only depend on the next hop toward the destination. Gradual deployment is then hard, because a router cannot tell where the next router that understands the new protocol is.

One approach is hop-by-hop forwarding toward the ultimate destination, assuming every system along the path understands the protocol, but that blocks phased deployment. RSVP instead puts the ultimate destination in the IP Destination Address field and asks every RSVP router to make a small change in its forwarding path to pull out RSVP packets and process them locally, which automatically tunnels through routers that do not understand RSVP. The cost may be unacceptable, because the mainline forwarding path of routers is highly tuned: even one extra instruction may cost hundreds of packets per second. The goal of this RFC is a way for routers to intercept such packets with no significant performance penalty.
sections.plainLanguage: New protocols need routers to notice certain special packets, but checking every packet would slow ordinary traffic. This RFC defines a marker that only the special packets carry.

sections.title: The Router Alert Option Format
sections.content:
The Router Alert option has the semantic that routers should examine this packet more closely. Its format is four octets: a type byte of 10010100, a length of 4, and a two-octet value. The type byte carries copied flag 1, meaning all fragments must carry the option, option class 0 (control) and option number 20 in decimal. In the value field, 0 means the router shall examine the packet, and 1 to 65535 are reserved.

Routers that support option processing in the fast path already demultiplex on the option type field. If all option types are supported there, one more type is unlikely to affect performance. If some types are not supported there, this option is unrecognized and such packets are kicked out into the slow path, so no change to the fast path is necessary and regular data packets pay no penalty. Routers with no fast-path option processing also forward such packets through the slow path.
sections.plainLanguage: The option is four bytes in the IP header: a type, a length, and a value. A value of zero means please examine this packet. All fragments of a packet carry the option.

sections.title: Semantics and Use
sections.content:
Hosts shall ignore the option. Routers that do not recognize the option shall ignore it. Routers that do recognize it shall examine packets carrying it more closely, for example by checking the IP Protocol field, to decide whether further processing is needed. Unrecognized value fields shall be silently ignored, and the meaning of other value field numbers is left for further study.

For the option to be effective, its use must be mandated in protocols that expect routers to perform significant processing on packets not directly addressed to them. The RFC names RSVP and IGMP as such protocols at the time of writing.
sections.plainLanguage: Hosts and ignorant routers leave the packet alone. A router that knows the option reads the packet more carefully, usually checking which protocol it carries. Protocols that need this must require the option in their own specifications.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The security discussion covers misuse in both directions. If the option is not set and should be set, the behavior of the protocol using it, such as RSVP or IGMPv2, is adversely affected, because that protocol relies on the option. If the option is set when it should not be, the flow likely takes a performance penalty, because the packet leaves the router's fast path and is processed more slowly than if the option were absent.
sections.plainLanguage: Leaving the marker off breaks the protocol that needs it. Putting the marker on needlessly slows that traffic down.

fields.name: Type
fields.desc: Copied flag 1, option class 0, option number 20.

fields.name: Value
fields.desc: 0 means router shall examine packet; 1-65535 reserved.
